title: Tennessee-based nonprofit group caught in Nepal flooding, 22 Americans among travelers - WTVC
description: Tennessee-based nonprofit group caught in Nepal flooding, 22 Americans among travelers  WTVC
publisher.title: WTVC
full_article:
McMINNVILLE, Tenn. — A Tennessee-connected nonprofit is working to account for dozens of Americans after a pilgrimage group was caught in catastrophic flooding near the Nepal-Tibet border.

Sadhguru Jaggi Vasudev, founder of the Isha Foundation, says about 80 people traveling with the group were caught in flash flooding near Mount Kailash, a destination considered sacred by several religions.

“We’ve sent messages to all the families,” Sadhguru said in a social media post.

Sadhguru says 22 of the travelers were from the United States.

People walk past damage in the aftermath of flash floods in Devighat in the Nuwakot district in Nepal, Thursday, Aug. 27, 2026. (AP Photo/Niranjan Shrestha)

Leslie Crespi, a community liaison for Isha Foundation’s McMinnville center, says those Americans were affiliated with the Tennessee-based non-profit.

“They're like family to us,” Crespi says. “These are people that we knew and we volunteered alongside of for many years.”

The group’s ordeal comes as widespread flooding across Nepal and neighboring China has left hundreds dead and more than 1,000 people missing.

Reports indicate at least 90 Americans are among those missing across the region as search and rescue efforts continue.

This satellite image provided by Vantor shows destruction at Syapru Besi, Nepal on Thursday, Aug. 27, 2026. (Satellite image ©2026 Vantor via AP)

The flooding and devastation are believed to be connected to a glacier.

UTC Assistant Professor of Geology Jennifer Taylor says glaciers can hold massive amounts of water...

“When you look at these glaciers, think of them as filling entire valleys,” Taylor says. “They are holding a lot of water in the first place.”

Jenisha, right, cries as she waits for news on her father missing after flash flooding in Nepal's Nuwakot district, Friday, Aug. 28, 2026. (AP Photo/Rajesh Kumar Singh)

Taylor says the region’s steep mountains can intensify flooding. The terrain can funnel water through narrow valleys, creating powerful and fast-moving walls of water

"That's where you're getting these very high, tall walls of water is because that water is not having a chance to spread out, but staying funneled in those really steep valleys."

This satellite image provided by Vantor shows the remains of a cement site in Nepal on Thursday, Aug. 27, 2026. (Satellite image 2026 Vantor via AP)

In a statement sent Friday evening, Isha Foundation says...

"Isha Foundation is deeply saddened by the devastating flash floods that have struck Gyirong in Tibet, near the Nepal-China border.

One of our Kailash Yatra groups was at the immigration center in Gyirong while returning from Kailash when the flash flood occurred. The immigration center and surrounding areas were severely impacted. At this time, we are awaiting official information regarding the whereabouts and wellbeing of those who were at the location...

Sadhguru, founder of Isha Foundation, along with volunteers across the globe and support teams in the region, is working closely with the concerned authorities and doing everything possible to support the ongoing search and rescue efforts. We request everyone to keep those affected in their thoughts and prayers and to rely only on verified updates from official sources. Our immediate priority is the safety and wellbeing of everyone affected. We are working urgently with relevant authorities and diplomatic representatives to confirm the status and whereabouts of those unaccounted for."

We have reached out to the Isha Foundation's base in McMinnville to discover if any of those Americans involved lived in Tennessee. So far we have not heard back yet.

Depend on us to keep you posted.

title: 'It stood like a serpent right there staring at us': American who survived deadly Nepal flood tells her story - ABC News - Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
description: 'It stood like a serpent right there staring at us': American who survived deadly Nepal flood tells her story  ABC News - Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
publisher.title: ABC News - Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
full_article:
KATHMANDU, NEPAL -- Anjana Raja had long dreamed of traveling to Nepal as part of a spiritual journey to Mount Kailash ever since she was a teenager, she said.

When she and her husband finally got to make that dream a reality this month, the California mom of two told ABC News she could not have imagined that trip would force them into survival mode as they found themselves nearly swept up in the deadly landslide flood that hit the region Wednesday.

Nepal survivor Anjana Raja speaks to ABC News. ABC News

Raja recalled sitting on a bus with her husband traveling to the Chinese border on Wednesday when, all of a sudden, the driver and front passengers fled the bus and she saw the landslide coming toward their vehicle.

Related Hundreds dead as over 2,000 remain missing in massive Nepal-Tibet flood

"It was water mixed with the mud that was a good 50 to 60 feet high. It stood like a serpent right there staring at us," Raja told ABC News. "Like a cobra's head staring at you."

Firefighters conduct a search and rescue operation at a damaged road leading to Gyirong Port after a mudslide, in Gyirong county, Shigatse, Tibet Autonomous Region, China, August 28, 2026. Cnsphoto via Reuters

Raja said she didn't hesitate and grabbed her sling bag and turned to her husband, Pattabiraman Venkatesan.

"I grabbed him by the collar, and I said, 'Run, we need to go right now,'" she said.

"I didn't even give time to act. I just said, 'Leave the bus right away or we're gonna die,'" Raja added.

A collapsed bridge and damaged settlements debris and mud covers an area following flash floods, August 28, 2026 in DeviGhat village, Nepal. Ritesh Shukla/Getty Images

As of Friday, as intense search and rescue efforts continue, 584 people have been reported dead in the floods, according to the Nepal National Disaster Management Authority and Chinese government.

Meanwhile, over 2,400 people were reported missing according to Nepal's National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority and the Chinese government.

Faced with the huge wall of water and mud, the couple and other bus passengers ran to a camp right next to the bus and made their way to higher ground as the water hit and completely flooded the streets, she said.

"We just blindly...climbed. We didn't even know what direction ... There was no guide for us, there was nobody, we were just frantically running. Running, literally running. It was slushy, it was muddy, we were climbing rocks, which was slippery. We just ran for our life," she said.

Popular Reads Lindsay Clancy trial: Jury being sent home for weekend 10 hours ago Iran live updates: As war nears 6 months, Trump continues to say Iran is 'failing' 1 day ago Iran updates: Iran officials push back against Trump's 'economic D-Day' threat Aug 23

"When we reached the second level ... I saw the water come up to the slope and move our bus. I told my husband 'That's it, we're gone. We're going to die,'" she said.

They ultimately made their way up to the third level of the camp and they watched in shock as the wall of water rushed past them.

From their point they could see vehicles, objects and even people be taken in by the water's power, although the water never reached their level.

"It just came like a roar, it sucked a bunch of buses, SUVs, people, the basecamp, everything -- took it in, turned it, turned it all upside down and dumped it into the ground," Raja said.

Residents salvage belongings from their destroyed home following flash floods, August 28, 2026 in Devighat, Nepal. Ezra Acayan/Getty Images

Eventually, Raja said she and her husband were able to contact her daughter Amanda, a physician, back in California and they have been in constant contact. The couple also has a college-age son.

Related What caused Nepal flood? Scientist says it was enormous landslide, glacier fall

Raja commended the actions of first responders, especially how they worked to take care of the most vulnerable victims.

"What I really loved is his focus was not foreign nationals, nor U.S. citizens. He looked at us as humans," she said of her rescuer.

Raja said that the entire experience has left a long-lasting impression on her.

"I know time will heal but I think, with all this what happened, I think I've become stronger mentally, emotionally. I'm not crying so that's a good thing," she said.

Nepal survivor Anjana Raja speaks to ABC News. ABC News

Still, Raja said she and her husband are determined to return and complete their journey to Mount Kailash.

"I am determined to," she said.

'The race is on' to try and find stranded school kids, Save The Children UK says published at 22:32 BST 28 August 22:32 BST 28 August

Image source, Reuters Image caption, Schoolchildren wait at an emergency centre in Trishuli to be transferred back to their home towns

George Graham of Save The Children UK says the charity's team in Nepal has been "working flat out" to rescue children, many of whom are stranded without their parents.

He tells the BBC News channel there are around "fifty children that we know of who are trapped in schools" who "may or may not have clean drinking water".

"The bridges that connect those schools to the roads have been washed away. The race is on to try and find those kids," he says.

"The flood came at the start of the school day," he says. "These children walk a long way from their homes to go to school, completely separate from their families."

Graham says they have rescued nine children so far who "walked a long way until they found our relief teams".

"They found themselves alone.. having to work out how to stay alive and stay safe," he says. The next job is working to reunite them with their families.

But there are "hundreds and hundreds of kids in this situation", he says.

title: Number of Australians missing in Nepal’s deadly floods rises again, as Albanese deploys more personnel - The Guardian
description: Number of Australians missing in Nepal’s deadly floods rises again, as Albanese deploys more personnel  The Guardian
publisher.title: The Guardian
full_article:
The number of Australians who were reported missing in the catastrophic Nepal flooding disaster has risen to 41, as one family celebrates after an unaccounted-for woman made contact with them yesterday.

It means three additional Australians were confirmed missing overnight – up from 38 who remained unaccounted for on Friday evening.

The Australian government’s Department of Foreign Affairs has been urgently working with local authorities to contact Australian woman Cara Severino, 25, who became the first Australian reported missing who has been confirmed safe.

‘So desperately loved’: ADF member among dozens of Australians missing in Nepal floods as families pray for safe return Read more

Severino contacted her parents, Debbie and Frank Severino, on Friday morning, informing them she was hiking away from the disaster zone to Kathmandu with a group of Nepali hikers – a trek of more than 110km.

Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email

The Red Cross has said about 600 people are dead and as many as 93,000 people may have been affected by Wednesday’s flash floods on the Nepal-Tibet border, with a huge rescue operation that is being hampered by fears of new flooding.

Dfat has received more than 450 calls in relation to the disaster.

View image in fullscreen Some of Australia’s missing in Nepal as of Friday, 28 August. Clockwise from left: Karan Bhardwaj, Chitra Venkatraman, Venkatraman Balakrishnan, Sumi Adhikari and family: Shylaja Muralitharan, Aarush Muralitharan, Ashwin Muralitharan & Chandrasekaran Muralitharan. Composite: Supplied by the families

Nepal’s disaster management agency says there are 1,924 people unaccounted for – 517 of those people are foreign tourists.

About 7:30pm on Friday evening, the authority said 121 foreigners had been rescued – none of them were Australians.

View from Kathmandu hospital

Outside the hospital in Kathmandu yesterday, there were scenes of anxiety as families put up posters of loved ones, and authorities hung pictures of the dead that need to be identified.

One woman said her cousin was on his way back from Australia because his brother had gone missing.

Nepal floods

Like many others, she was putting pictures of him up, in case he was brought back to the hospital.

Australian charities are starting to pump in aid, with the Emergency Action Alliance – a peak body representing major Australian charities – raising funds to build emergency shelters, get food and safe drinking water, hygiene supplies and medical care to communities.

At least 93,000 ‘in great need’ after Nepal-Tibet flash floods, says Red Cross Read more

But conditions on the ground are difficult and unpredictable owing to the scale of the damage and the heavy monsoon. Rescue operations in Nepal and China resumed as of Saturday morning after being suspended due to the risk of further flooding.

“The gravity of the situation is worse now because whole towns have swept away,” Australian Nepalese Multicultural Centre vice president Keshav Kadel said.

“Now there is nothing, it’s just a mudslide.”

View image in fullscreen An aerial view shows the aftermath of massive flooding along the Bhotekoshi River, which affected low-lying areas and settlements near the riverbanks in Nuwakot, Nepal. Photograph: Ap Tolang/Nexpher/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock

View image in fullscreen The flooding caused widespread damage to homes, roads, bridge, hydropower station and other infrastructure in the area. Photograph: Ap Tolang/Nexpher/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock

Four Dfat crisis response team officers are expected to arrive in Kathmandu later on Saturday to support consular efforts on the ground.

Four rapid response team members are also expected to arrive in Kathmandu – humanitarian response specialists with expertise in communications, logistics and planning.

These extra deployments add to about 20 personnel Australian already has on the ground with the Australian embassy in Kathmandu.

How the deadly Nepal and Tibet flash flood unfolded – a visual guide Read more

On Friday night, the foreign affairs minister, Penny Wong, spoke with the Nepali foreign minister, Shisir Khanal, to affirm that Australia would provide further humanitarian assistance, including to aid rescue and recovery efforts, where required.

Australia has pledged $5m in aid and support for the disaster, with $2m going to the World Food Programme to provide emergency food and water provisions, and the remaining to the Emergency Action Alliance.

Australia’s assistant minister for foreign affairs and trade, Matt Thistlethwaite, said on Saturday morning that the aid was being provided on request of the Nepalese authorities. Speaking to ABC News Breakfast, Thistlethwaite said Australian officials in Beijing were also working with the Chinese Government, but that China had not so far requested support.

“We’re doing our best to support both the Nepalese and Tibetan diasporas here in Australia,” Thistlethwaite said.

“Yesterday I held two online forums, one with the Nepalese community one with the Tibetan community to outline the latest situation, to advise of the support that Australia is providing, the $5m in humanitarian aid, and the best way for us to keep in contact with them. We’re providing them with the latest information through our officials.

“I also attended a vigil last night with the Nepalese community in Strathfield and obviously there was quite a bit of despair and anxiety in that community, but we’re doing our best to support the Tibetan and Nepalese communities here in Australia.”

title: Pope Leo prays for victims of devastating Nepal floods - Vatican News
description: Pope Leo prays for victims of devastating Nepal floods  Vatican News
publisher.title: Vatican News
full_article:
Vatican News

Pope Leo XIV has expressed his deep sorrow over the loss of life and widespread devastation caused by flash floods in Nepal.

In a telegram sent on Thursday and signed by Cardinal Secretary of State Pietro Parolin, the Pope commended the souls of those who died “to the clemency of the Almighty” and offered his heartfelt condolences to the bereaved.

He also assured all those affected by the disaster of his spiritual closeness and prayed for the emergency personnel engaged in the ongoing search-and-rescue operations.

The telegram concluded with the Pope's prayers for God’s assistance and protection upon the people of Nepal.

Hundreds dead or missing

Over 350 people have died in Nepal, while more than 900 remain unaccounted for after a devastating torrent of water, mud and debris swept through communities near the country’s northern border with China. Unfortunately, the death toll is expected to rise as bodies are recovered from under the debris.

Hundreds more are missing in neighbouring Tibet, bringing the total number of people unaccounted for across the affected region to almost 1,500.

The disaster is believed to have been triggered by the collapse of part of a Himalayan glacier, which sent a sudden surge into a river system along the Nepal-China border. Scientists said the force of the collapse was so great that the resulting tremors were initially mistaken for an earthquake.

Entire settlements were inundated, while roads, bridges, power installations and other essential infrastructure were destroyed or severely damaged. The floods also struck a major border crossing, cutting off transport and trade routes.

Many of those missing are foreign visitors who had travelled to the region on pilgrimage to Mount Kailash and Lake Mansarovar, sites considered sacred by Hindus, Buddhists, Jains and followers of the Bon religion.

Rescue operations continue

Thousands of soldiers, police officers and emergency workers have been deployed across the affected areas. Helicopters are being used to reach isolated communities, evacuate survivors and deliver food, medical supplies and other forms of emergency assistance.

Operations are being complicated by damaged roads, difficult mountainous terrain and the continuing danger of landslides and further flooding.

International aid has begun to arrive, with neighbouring countries, the United Nations and humanitarian organisations offering personnel, supplies and financial assistance.

The tragedy has also renewed concerns about the growing threat posed by glacial instability in the Himalayas, where rising temperatures are accelerating the melting and retreat of glaciers.

पड़ोसी देश तिब्बत म॑ सैकड़ों आरू लोगऽ के लापता छै, जेकरा स॑ पूरा प्रभावित क्षेत्र म॑ बेहिसाब लोगऽ के संख्या लगभग १५०० होय गेलऽ छै ।

मानल जा रहल अछि जे ई आपदा हिमालयी ग्लेशियर के किछु हिस्सा के ढहला सं भेल अछि, जाहि सं नेपाल-चीन सीमा पर नदी प्रणाली मे अचानक उफान आबि गेल. वैज्ञानिक सब के कहनाय छनि जे एहि गिरय के बल एतेक बेसी छल जे एकर परिणामस्वरूप बनल भूकंप के शुरू मे भूकंप के गलती सं मानल गेल छल.

title: Nepal and China resume flood rescue as death toll nears 600 - Al Jazeera
description: Nepal and China resume flood rescue as death toll nears 600  Al Jazeera
publisher.title: Al Jazeera
full_article:
Rescuers are continuing efforts in the flood-ravaged Nepal-Tibet border region after a brief pause over fears of a second glacial flood.

Nepal’s police said the number of people killed in the disaster has risen to 626, with the country’s disaster authority reporting at least 1,924 people missing.

Recommended Stories list of 2 items list 1 of 2 8-year-old Nepal flood survivor reunited with mother after rescue

8-year-old Nepal flood survivor reunited with mother after rescue list 2 of 2 Before and after images show catastrophic impact of Nepal flash floods end of list

Chinese authorities have reported that the death toll in Tibet has now risen to at least seven, with 558 people missing.

Al Jazeera’s Minelle Fernandez, reporting from the Nepalese capital, Kathmandu, said the government has requested specialist help from India and China to “fill gaps” in its rescue operations. Those teams, which includes tunnel rescue, are expected to arrive later on Saturday.

“The reason the [Nepalese] foreign ministry spokesman said that this decision has been taken is because lives are at stake and that it is very, very urgent,” she said.

“The reason that initially Nepal had said they didn’t want assistance is they didn’t want the chaos which comes with huge teams being fanned out in different areas.”

The catastrophe began on Wednesday morning when part of a glacier collapsed at roughly 5,200 metres in the Himalayas, plunging about 1,200 metres and gathering rock and debris before slamming into the Lende River.

The resulting surge swept south through Nepal’s Rasuwa, Nuwakot and Dhading districts, at one point raising the Trishuli River by 9 metres in 30 minutes. The US Geological Survey revised its initial finding of an earthquake trigger, concluding the seismic signal instead came from the landslide itself.

Advertisement

A new lake formed at the collapse site and began rising afterwards, prompting a temporary halt to search efforts amid fears of a second flood. Operations have now resumed after the lake’s risks were deemed manageable.

Alton Byers, a glacial-hazards scientist at the University of Colorado Boulder’s Institute of Arctic and Alpine Research, told Al Jazeera that the barrier holding back the new lake is highly unstable, made up of loose debris that had cascaded into place two days earlier, and that there is “not much holding it”.

Byers said the safest outcome would be a natural, gradual drainage, noting that Chinese crews could also try to lower the lake using hand tools and other methods manually – a technique he said has been used in other countries prone to glacial lake outburst floods.

Chinese Premier Li Qiang visited the disaster zone in Gyirong on Thursday, and President Xi Jinping chaired a meeting ordering officials to “scientifically formulate search-and-rescue plans” and strengthen monitoring of glacial lakes, according to state media.

International aid has arrived from India, the UN, the Red Cross Federation, Australia, South Korea and the US. Officials warn the death toll will likely keep rising as rescuers reach areas still cut off by mud and washed-out roads.

1. Himalayan Glacier Adventures group Fifteen of the missing Australians were on a pilgrimage with the Himalayan Glacier tour group to Mount Kailash in Tibet, which is a sacred site for Hindus, Buddhists, Jains and the Bon faith. All but one in the group are Sydney-based members of the Australia Bharatha Brahmin Samaj community. Number of Australians missing in Nepal’s deadly floods rises again, as Albanese deploys more personnel Read more Among those unaccounted for are NSW couple Venkatraman Balakrishnan, 52, and Chitra Venkatraman, 46, as well as Sreedharan and Lakshmi Iyer, and their adult sons Rishab, 23, and Rudhra, 20. The Iyer brothers are medical students at the University of Newcastle and members of the West Pennant Hills Cherrybrook cricket club in Sydney’s north-west. “WPHCCC is aware of the reports that two of our players, Rishab and Rudhra Iyer, along with their family members and other Australians, are unaccounted for in the ongoing floods in Nepal,” the club said in a statement. “We continue to live in hope, and our thoughts are currently with them, their loved ones and all affected by this tragedy in Nepal.” Also in the group is a family of four: Shylaja Muralitharan, 42, her husband, Chandrasekaran Muralitharan, 47, and their sons Ashwin, 14, and Aarush, 11. Shylaja’s sister, Vaishnavi, said she had lost contact with the family on the morning of the flood as the family prepared to cross an immigration checkpoint at the Tibet-Nepal border. “Just like everyone else that’s part of that group, we’re really worried, but hopeful,” Vaishnavi said. “Hopeful that they’re safe and just waiting to be rescued. “It’s a very difficult time for our whole family.” Sagar Pandey, founder and chief executive of Himalayan Glacier Adventures, said he had lost all contact with his tour group of 47 people. Pandey said on Thursday he had flown by helicopter over the Rasuwa area where the group was staying and had little hope they survived. 2. Kailash Journeys tour group Six Australians are missing from a tour group with Kailash Journeys. Among them is Karan Bhardwaj, a 40-year-old Brisbane-based member of the Royal Australian Air Force. At least 93,000 ‘in great need’ after Nepal-Tibet flash floods, says Red Cross Read more “Karan is a dad to my beautiful seven-year-old nephew, as well as a brother, uncle and brother in law,” said his family member Jen. “He is so desperately loved by his family and right now we are desperately praying, hoping and believing that Karan is safe, alive and somehow making his way back to us.” 3. Narayan Panthi Narayan Panthi, from Brisbane, has been listed by Nepalese police as travelling with operator Kathmandu Holiday Tours and Travel. It is understood Panthi had been carrying out independent volunteer charity work in Kathmandu earlier in the week before travelling towards the border region. Panthi’s cousin, Amrit Bhusal, told Guardian Australia his family was devastated but “holding on to hope and praying for positive news”.



“We are still hoping,” Bhusal said. “We are still searching. We are still praying for Narayan to come home safely.”



Bhusal said Panthi was “helping disadvantaged children in Nepal reach their full potential through education”. 4. Isha Foundation A group of 11 Australians remain missing after travelling with an Isha Foundation pilgrimage. The foundation confirmed that 11 Australians among a group of 80 missing pilgrims, were inside an immigration building at the Gyirong border crossing when the flood hit. Among them, Guardian Australia has confirmed, is missing Australian woman Sumi Adhikari. Her husband, Nava Pandey, has travelled to Nepal seeking information about her whereabouts. “We still have no clear or official information about Sumi or the other members of her group,” Pandey said on Saturday morning. Also missing is 42-year-old Australian man Bharat Mangwani, who was travelling with the Isha Foundation as part of a pilgrimage to Lake Manasarovar when his family lost contact with him on Wednesday morning. He was last seen at Gyirong before the group was set to depart for Kathmandu. Mangwani’s family, including his nine-year-old son and three-year-old daughter, have travelled to India with a family friend, while his wife has travelled to Nepal to search.

title: Chinese rescuers find ‘nothing but ruins’ at border crossing as Nepal seeks help to ID and store the dead - The Guardian
description: Chinese rescuers find ‘nothing but ruins’ at border crossing as Nepal seeks help to ID and store the dead  The Guardian
publisher.title: The Guardian
full_article:
A Chinese rescue team has reached the all-but-obliterated Gyirong border crossing complex for the first time and found “nothing but ruins” as Nepal and China continue their arduous rescue operations in the flood-hit Himalayas.

Surveillance camera footage from the worst-hit Gyirong border crossing complex showed huge torrents of water and debris on Wednesday engulfing buildings and people trying to flee. Only ⁠on Friday were rescuers able to reach that area.

State media reported that the Chinese team of 21 rescuers and a search-and-rescue dog crossed mountains and valleys and used ropes to navigate forests and cliffs after roads to the complex, hemmed in by steep Himalayan slopes, were destroyed.

‘The flood took everything I have’: survivors grieve for relatives and homes swept away in Nepal Read more

“There was no road … it was all virgin forest and sheer cliffs,” rescue worker Zou Mingqi said. At the complex, “as far as the eye could ⁠see, there was nothing but ruins.”

The glacier collapse which unleashed a deadly torrent through Himalayan mountain river systems has killed at least 616 people ⁠in Nepal and seven in China’s Tibet. The number of ⁠missing in Nepal has nearly doubled to 1,924, officials said on Friday. At least 558 were missing in Tibet’s Gyirong County, Chinese state media said. Among the missing were at least 540 foreigners, many of them Hindu pilgrims from India.

Amid the deepening crisis, Nepal has now said it needs foreign ⁠help in specialised and technical areas in which it does not have expertise, but not in search and rescue.

Earlier on ⁠Friday, Nepal’s foreign ministry had said that Kathmandu could manage ​the rescue ​efforts on its own for ​now and declined foreign involvement.

The areas Nepal is seeking help include opening transport and communication services in places where bridges have been destroyed, identification of dead bodies, DNA testing and storing bodies for longer durations, foreign minister Shisir Khanal said late on Friday.

Asked about that stance of ​his government, ‌Khanal said ​there was no ​need for assistance in general search and rescue which was being done by Nepali rescuers. “We think there is no need for repetition in this,” he said.

India and ​China, between whom Nepal is wedged, have been requested to supply bailey bridges to reopen transport and communication in an area where about two dozen bridges had been destroyed.

View image in fullscreen A woman salvages usable materials from her house deluged in sludge following flash floods at Devighat in Nepal’s Nuwakot district. Photograph: AFP/Getty Images

Nepal is continuing to monitor two barrier lakes upstream of the flood zone, with an official warning that flood risks will persist until both lakes fully drain.

Satellite imagery showed the second lake growing larger with no visible outlet, raising concerns that water pressure could still be building.

China’s state-run Xinhua news agency said that the first barrier lake was reducing in size, citing analysis by the water resources ministry. A Chinese government geo-hazards expert warned, however, that the lake may be ‌unstable and that over 100 glacial lakes scattered throughout the area could pose a threat.

Map of key locations affected by the flash floods

In Beijing, a politburo meeting chaired by President Xi Jinping called for stronger monitoring of glacier lakes and landslide risks, and for closer international disaster cooperation, Xinhua reported.

China’s Premier Li Qiang, the country’s No. 2 official, arrived in the area of Gyirong on Thursday afternoon, Xinhua said. The visit suggested Beijing was treating the disaster as a matter of ​the highest national priority.

In China, strict controls on the flow of information from one of its most sensitive regions are hampering the public’s understanding of events.

On the ground in Nepal after deadly flash floods – video

The BBC and New York Times have reported videos of the catastrophic floods, widely shared globally, have not appeared on Chinese social media sites.

Chinese state media has carried several broadcasts about the floods and dispatched their own journalists to the area, but reports have focused on the rescue efforts rather than the scale of the devastation. In one broadcast from a relief centre in Tibet, the journalist did not speak to any of the people sitting behind him.

Tibet, brought under Chinese control in the 1950s, is the most sensitive and tightly controlled region in the country.

The Gyirong border port plays a key role in China’s Belt and Road network linking the country to South Asia, with logistics zones and parking lots built there in the past decade.

Nepal’s finance minister, Swarnim Wagle, estimated the country will ⁠need $4bn – $5bn for rebuilding. “This is just an ​estimate. Loss and ⁠damage is ​being assessed,” he ​said.

More than 90,000 people have been affected by the disaster, the Red Cross estimated.

title: US families with relatives missing in the Nepal-China floods plead for more rescue help - AP News

Mukti Patel has huddled with family and friends at her parents’ Richmond, Virginia, home since her dad, sister and two other relatives went missing in the catastrophic flash floods along the Nepal-China border.

She knows the hotel they were staying in was swept away. But as she shared memories of them on Friday, she caught herself.

“I shouldn’t talk in past tense yet,” she said. “We don’t know anything.”

As rescuers continued pulling survivors from the mud , family members of some of the more than 2,000 people missing in the disaster were still holding out hope — however dim — that their loved ones survived.

On a Zoom call Thursday night, some family members wanted to know if they could reach the site and whether a relative might be trapped inside an air pocket, said Sanket Pandey, managing director of Himalayan Glacier Adventure and Travel Company.

Ishan Patel turned 32 on Wednesday, and the family called to wish him a happy birthday. That was their last contact.

Mukti Patel said she would like more countries to help the rescue and recovery efforts .

Jiwan Jyoti, who has U.S. citizenship, also was traveling with Himalayan Glacier and was listed by the group as missing. They had stopped in Timure, Nepal, before they were set to leave for a pilgrimage to Mount Kailash in Tibet, a sacred site for Hindus, Buddhists and others, her longtime friend Manmeet Singh Meet said.

Jyoti, a 50-year-old from Lexington, Massachusetts, called her family from breakfast on Wednesday as she was preparing to cross into Tibet.

Meet said the phone call ended “at around 8:40 a.m. local time in Nepal, and then I think around 8:45, this flash floods came, and then our world turned upside down.”

He later heard that the hotel where Jyoti had been staying — and where her location was last recorded on the Find My iPhone app — was destroyed. Now Meet said he is losing hope that his best friend of 15 years will be found alive.

“She was essentially almost in the epicenter over there,” Meet said.

Vaasavi Unnava, a 31-year-old PhD student, thought her parents had already crossed into Tibet with the same tour group when she learned about the flooding.

“I was not really that worried, but I just sent them a text like to be sure,” she said. The WhatsApp message didn’t get delivered.

Her father, Hanumantha Rao Unnava, and mother, Vasundhara Unnava, had set out on a retirement trip and were most excited to go spend two months in India with family after going to Mount Kailash. The couple from Woodland, California, is among dozens of U.S. citizens missing in the flood.

“They were so, so excited. My dad was talking about finally getting to spend time with his mother,” Vaasavi Unnava said.

Until recently, her father was the dean of the Graduate School of Management at the University of California, Davis, and her mother lectured at the university, she said. Vaasavi Unnava described her dad as “disciplined and duty-bound” but also “a big joker.” She described her mom as “spontaneous and playful” and “the smartest woman I’ve ever met.”

The flash flood disaster in Nepal has been witnessed by the whole world, through videos circulating online, carrying footage of massive floods. Houses destroyed. People killed, swept away in the water. Cities and buildings, everything, vanishing in minutes. But natural disasters often leave behind remarkable stories of survival. Amid the devastation caused by the flash floods in Nepal, one such escape caught attention online.

A video showing a green-painted house surrounded by fast-moving, muddy floodwaters went viral after viewers spotted a family trapped inside the building. According to the first viral video of the green house, as the floodwaters surged through the area, several structures around the house appeared to be swept away.

The footage showed the force of the floodwaters carrying debris and destroying buildings in their path. However, as per a latest video of the same green house, it remained standing despite being surrounded by the raging water.

The video prompted widespread concern for the family inside the house, with social media users praying for their safety as they watched the frightening scenes unfold.

full_article:
KATHMANDU, Nepal (AP) — Poor weather hampered aerial rescue operations in Nepal on Saturday as the search for thousands of missing people in areas devastated by catastrophic flash floods along the border with China entered its fourth day.

Rescue workers and military personnel have been working around the clock since Wednesday’s disaster, which killed more than 600 people and left about 3,000 missing. Some survivors have been pulled from the mud , while crews continue searching several locations for those still missing.

But Brig. Gen. Raja Ram Basnet, a Nepali Army spokesperson, said Saturday that helicopter operations were on hold until weather conditions improved.

Search and rescue efforts continued at several locations in Nepal and China’s Tibet, including the Upper Trishuli-1 Hydropower Project in Nepal’s Rasuwa district and the severely damaged Gyirong border crossing on the Chinese side.

Basnet said rescuers had used baskets and ropes to reach some people, but the operation remained difficult because of 4 to 5 feet (1.2 to 1.5 meters) of mud and the limited number of places where helicopters could land.

Search continues at devastated China-Nepal border crossing

The broadcaster was showing Saturday images of rescuers getting to Gyirong Port, the hard-hit border crossing with Nepal. Some reached the area by foot and via rafts. Some were dropped down from drones flown to the area. “Anyone, anyone?” rescuers yelled, according to footage by the broadcaster.

It was not immediately known how many people were at the border checkpoint building when the floods hit.

On Saturday, Nepal’s disaster agency said the death toll had climbed to 626 with 2,426 people missing in the country. There was little information on survivors on the Chinese side, where the death toll rose to seven Friday as state media showed evacuations of villages and leaders’ efforts to direct the relief response.

More than 3,700 people have been rescued in Nepal so far. China’s state media said 554 people were missing on the Chinese side. Hundreds of the missing are foreigners who were in the area to work, trek or make a pilgrimage to a sacred peak .

title: Son of us couple who narrowly escaped Nepal flood ‘grateful for the miracle’ - CNN
description: Son of us couple who narrowly escaped Nepal flood ‘grateful for the miracle’  CNN
publisher.title: CNN
full_article: The son of an American couple who survived the devastating floods in Nepal is preparing to reunite with his parents. Looking ahead to the reunion, his mother told CNN, "I'm going to hug them and cry because I am an emotional mama." Her son, Vikram Ravi, reflected on the harrowing ordeal, telling Brianna Keilar, "I'm just thankful that I was able to hear her tell me that she's okay, rather than having to go look for her."
